1:
The chapter turns on a sleepless night, and the witnesses agree that nothing in it is accident. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene against the plot of the chapter before: as Satan had put it into Haman’s heart to contrive Mordecai’s death, so now God puts it into the king’s heart to contrive Mordecai’s honour; and where both God and the king will have a man honoured, it is to no purpose for Haman to oppose it. “His sleep fled away,” Henry renders the Hebrew — and like a shadow, the more the king pursued it the further it withdrew; he who commanded a hundred and twenty-seven provinces could not command one hour’s sleep, for God, whose gift sleep is, withheld it. Henry even hears an offended conscience in the wakefulness, reproaching the king for having banished Esther from his presence above thirty days.

The reformed John Gill guards the same point against every natural cause: it was not anxious thought of his neglect of Esther, nor jealousy of Haman, nor fear of a conspiracy that kept him awake, but the overruling providence of God — a thing Jarchi was willing to call a miracle. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the theme of the whole book in a sentence: “God Himself is here, though His name be absent.” Looking at the matter in its merely human aspect, it was by a mere chance that the king called for the royal chronicles rather than for music, and a mere chance that the reader lit upon the record of Mordecai; yet woven together these seeming accidents make a providence that uses men whether they know it or not. He adds, on Rawlinson’s authority, that the Persian kings were in most cases unable to read, so that the book had to be read aloud before him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the unexpected turn: unable to sleep, the king had the book of records read to him, and the account of the conspiracy Mordecai had discovered — entered long before at Esther 2:23 — was thus brought before him, so that he asked whether the man had ever been rewarded. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the doctrine plainly: how vain are the contrivances of foolish man against the wise and omnipotent God, who has the hearts and hands of kings perfectly at his disposal and can by such trivial accidents change their minds; the troubled king, who might have diverted himself with his wives or with music, was moved instead to this reading. Adam Clarke, also wesleyan-arminian, reports the Targum’s tradition that the king had been warned in a dream that Haman meant to slay him and seize his throne, and observes that Persian chronicles, being poetry rather than dry annals, were in truth a likely thing to soothe a restless mind.
2:
What the reading uncovered was a debt the crown had forgotten. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that it was “found written” how Mordecai had given information against the two courtiers, Bigthana and Teresh, keepers of the door, who had sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus — the very conspiracy already related at Esther 2:21-23, where the first of the pair is named Bigthan. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is content to point the reader back to that earlier scene, where the service now recalled had first been rendered.

The reformed John Gill sees a peculiar hand of providence in the very passage the reader happened upon, and preserves a vivid tradition from the later Targum. Shimshai the scribe, ordered to bring the book and read — himself, the tradition says, a son of Haman — saw what stood written of Mordecai and turned the leaves over, unwilling to read it aloud; but the leaves rolled back of themselves, and he was forced to read that paragraph. Gill sees a peculiar hand of God in this too, directing the reader to that very portion of the annals among so many others, so that neither the recording of the deed nor the reading of it was left to chance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry tells the same wonder and draws its lesson. Mordecai was in no such favour at court that the reader should designedly pitch upon that place; rather providence directed him to it. Henry relays the tradition, as bishop Patrick reports it, that when the reader would have turned to some other part of the book the leaves flew back to the place where it had fallen open, so that he was compelled to read of Mordecai’s good service. That service — the discovery of the plot that saved the king’s life — had been faithfully entered in the record long before, at Esther 2:23, and here it is found upon record still, waiting for the hour when it should count. And here, Henry adds, is the comfort of a wakeful providence: the God who rules the smallest concerns of men, without whom not a sparrow falls to the ground, had so ordered the annals of a heathen empire that on this night of all nights the king’s ear should fall upon the one deed that would undo Haman. It is worth marking how long the interval had run between the service and its notice: the plot was foiled and faithfully entered, and there the matter had rested, the deliverer forgotten while the record slept — until the one night the king could not. The witnesses do not divide. Whether they credit the flying leaves to pious legend or simply marvel at the timing, they read one truth from the open page: a forgotten kindness, recorded and then left unrewarded, is remembered at the precise moment its remembrance will save a people.
3:
The king’s question — “What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this?” — and the servants’ bare answer, “There is nothing done for him,” open a meditation on gratitude and neglect. The reformed John Gill reads the king as judging the deed worthy of reward, the saving of his own life, yet unable to recall whether any favour had ever been shown for it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the terms: the king asks what greatness, what promotion to honour, had been done “for this,” for the giving of the information; and the servants reply that nothing whatever has been shown him. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, adds the Persian background: the names of those accounted “royal benefactors” were enrolled on a special list and were supposed to be suitably rewarded, so that the benefactor held an almost legal claim to recompense — a claim, in Mordecai’s case, long left unhonoured.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh why the debt went unpaid. Adam Clarke observes that the king plainly found nothing in the record, though the register of the chronicles was the very place such a reward would have been entered. John Wesley offers three reasons for the neglect: it might have happened through the king’s forgetfulness, or through the envy of the courtiers, or because Mordecai was a Jew, and therefore odious and contemptible in their eyes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the king’s enquiry into a mirror. The law of gratitude, he says, is a law of nature, and two rules may be gathered from the question: better honour than nothing, for if we cannot recompense those who have served us we may at least own our obligation; and better late than never, for a long-neglected debt should still at length be paid — the king remembering Mordecai as Pharaoh’s butler at last remembered Joseph, confessing his fault, as at Genesis 41:9. Yet Henry marks how often the best services go unrewarded among men: it is common for the great to take little notice of their inferiors, and humility, though of great price in God’s account, commonly hinders men’s preferment in the world, for honour makes the proud giddy but upholds the humble in spirit, as Proverbs 29:23 teaches. Little honour is done to those who best deserve it and would do most good with it, as the poor wise man of Ecclesiastes 9:14-16 was forgotten though he saved the city. Nay, Henry adds the sharpest irony: good service is sometimes so far from being a man’s preferment that it will not be his protection — for at this very hour Mordecai stands, by the king’s own edict, doomed to destruction with all the Jews, though it is here owned that he had deserved dignity.
4:
Morning comes, and with it a collision the actors cannot yet see. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the king’s abrupt “Who is in the court?” — wishing to repair the neglect and to honour the man who had done him service, as the Persian monarchs were wont to do, he looks for some minister with whom to take counsel; those who sought an audience waited in the outer court until summoned, and the very question shows that it was already morning. And Haman, the writer notes in parenthesis, had just then come into that outer court — to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows he had made ready. Charles Ellicott sets the two men in their places with grim symmetry: the king in the inner court ponders what recompense to bestow upon Mordecai, while Haman in the outer court stands primed with a request that the same man be hanged.

The reformed John Gill reads the king as simply in haste to confer some honour on Mordecai for what he had done. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fasten on Haman’s haste of another kind. John Wesley judges that he had come thus early because his malice would not suffer him to sleep, and was resolved to seize the very first opportunity of speaking before the king was engaged in other matters, waiting in the outer court because it was death to enter the inner without special license, as Esther 4:11 had shown. Adam Clarke agrees that this must have been very early, Haman’s pride and revenge both on the tenters to be gratified, and he sees the scene as fitting the Targum’s dream, in which the king was forewarned that Haman would come at dawn to ask for the life of the man who had rescued him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the irony the others sketch. Haman is so impatient to get Mordecai hanged that he comes early to court, to be ready at the king’s rising before any other business is brought in, so confident of his request that he has already built the gallows — one word from the king, he thinks, will complete his satisfaction. But the king is as impatient to have Mordecai honoured, and it is fit that the king, whose heart is full of the same man, should speak first. Neither knows the other’s errand; and providence has so timed their meeting that the courtier who came to procure a death will be made the herald of an honour.
5:
The answer to the king’s question sets the trap in motion. The reformed John Gill notes precisely where Haman was standing: in the outward court, for into the inner court none might enter unbidden, and there he waited for the summons he was so eager to receive. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the exchange with equal economy — the attendants tell the king that Haman is in the court, and the king commands, “Let him come in.”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in that brief command a whole web of unwitting design. Haman, says the king, is the fittest man to be employed both in directing and in dispensing the royal favour — and the king knew nothing of any quarrel between him and Mordecai, so that the very man who hated Mordecai above all others is the one now called in to devise his honour. It is the mark of the story’s irony, Henry lets us feel, that the king should reckon Haman the meetest instrument of a favourite’s honour at the moment Haman reckons himself the favourite and Mordecai a corpse-in-waiting. Haman is brought in immediately, proud of the distinction of being admitted into the king’s presence, as it should seem before the king had risen; and he comes swollen with the certainty that his own suit cannot fail. Indeed, Henry observes, the king would have Mordecai dignified that his own mind might be eased and he himself compose again to sleep, so that even the royal restlessness bends unawares toward the honour of the neglected man. Henry lets the reader feel how completely the two purposes cross: Haman thinks he has the fairest opportunity he could wish to solicit against Mordecai, but the king’s mind is as full as his, and it is fit the king should speak first. Every step Haman takes toward the throne in the confidence of his malice carries him nearer to the humiliation prepared for him — the eagerness that brought him early to court, the readiness that kept him waiting, the pride that swells at the summons, all of it serving a design he cannot see. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the plain course of the scene, Haman waiting and then admitted; Henry reads in it the quiet mastery of a providence that grants the enemy of God’s people exactly the access he craves, only to make that access the instrument of his own overthrow. The door opens at Haman’s wish, and he walks through it to his ruin.
6:
Haman enters, and before he can speak his errand the king’s question forestalls him. The reformed John Gill marks the timing: Haman came in, but was prevented from opening the business he came upon by the king’s own words. Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, sharpens the point — the king did not give him time to make his request, but put to him a question which, at first hearing, seemed to promise all that his heart could wish. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the words their literal force: not merely “whom the king delighteth to honour,” but “the man in whose honour the king delighteth.”

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley together explain the fatal ambiguity. The king, Wesley notes, names no one, that he might have the more impartial answer, and probably knew nothing of the quarrel between Haman and Mordecai; while Haman, thinking in his heart — the phrase Keil renders “to say within oneself” — asked, “To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?” He had, Wesley concedes, great reason to think so, given the favour the king had lately shown him above all others; and Keil catches the surpassing pride in the very grammar of his self-comparison, honour heaped beyond himself being to Haman unimaginable.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry both commends the king and exposes the courtier. It is a good property in kings and all superiors, he says, to delight in bestowing rewards and not in punishing; parents and masters should take pleasure in commending what is good in those under their charge. But Haman’s answer betrays how men’s pride deceives them. He had a better opinion of his own merits than there was cause for, thinking none so worthy of honour as himself — a foolish thing, for the deceitfulness of our own hearts appears in nothing so much as in the good conceit we have of ourselves. And he had a better opinion of his interest than there was reason for, imagining the king loved and valued none but him. Henry turns it to a warning we should watch and pray against: to suspect that the esteem others profess for us is less than it seems, lest we think too well of ourselves or trust too much in others. Haman, supposing he carves out honour for himself, is in truth measuring the reward of the man he means to hang.
7:
Haman’s reply comes without a pause, and the two witnesses who linger here catch both its haste and its reach. The reformed John Gill hears in the promptness the whole of the man: Haman answered the king “at once,” being very forward to suggest the honours he hoped to see done to himself. There is no deliberation, no feigned modesty, no asking who the favoured man might be — the vizier’s imagination has already seated him in the place of glory, and the words tumble out to furnish it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the sentence unfold to its full, immoderate length. For the man in whose honour the king delights, Haman begins, let them bring the royal apparel which the king has himself worn, and the horse on which the king has ridden, and the crown royal set upon his head; and let the apparel and horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king’s chief and noble princes, that they may array the man withal and bring him on horseback through the street of the city, proclaiming before him, “Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.” Keil marks that Haman votes at once for the very highest and most public mark of respect the realm could show, as though a subject’s honour could not be pressed too far.

The witnesses do not divide, and the shape of the answer tells its own tale. Every article Haman names is the king’s own — the king’s robe, the king’s horse, the king’s crown, a prince of the king’s court for a footman — so that what he asks is nothing less than to be treated, for a day, as the king himself. Keil marks the last stroke of the design: the very highest of the realm, one of the king’s chief and noble princes, is to be reduced to a lackey walking at the honoured man’s stirrup, so total is the elevation Haman covets that even the grandees must serve it. Gill’s single word, that he was “prompt,” and Keil’s careful inventory meet in one portrait: a man so certain that he is the intended favourite that he spends his whole invention on gilding his own triumph, never dreaming that he is drafting, in loving detail, the ceremony of his rival’s exaltation and his own disgrace. The very fulness of the request, offered so eagerly, becomes the measure of the fall that waits at the end of the sentence.
8:
The first item Haman names is the king’s own robe, and the witnesses gather to show how audacious the request was. The reformed John Gill explains that this was no ordinary suit but a single royal garment, the purple such as kings wore; among the Persians it was a capital crime to wear any of the king’s apparel. He recalls how Trebazus, an intimate of Artaxerxes, begged an old robe of the king and was granted it only on condition he never wear it, yet appeared in it at court to the outrage of the Persians; and how Artabanus, though uncle to Xerxes, was most unwilling to obey the order to put on the royal robes — so daring, Gill says, was this proposal of Haman’s. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley identifies the garment as the king’s outward robe of purple, interwoven with gold, as Justin and Curtius relate.

Adam Clarke, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, reads the whole demand as pride and folly walking hand in hand: the royal apparel was never worn but by the king, and even when he had laid it aside it was death for another to put it on, so that Haman, reaching for the very pinnacle of honour, never reflected that the higher he rose the more terrible his fall would be. Charles Ellicott presses the vanity further — nothing is said of any service Haman had rendered, yet so inordinate is his self-conceit that he cannot conceive the king to mean anyone but himself, and in a moment he is irretrievably committed. He illustrates the request from Herodotus, where Xerxes permits his uncle Artabanus to put on the royal robes and sleep in the royal bed, and the horse from Joseph riding in Pharaoh’s chariot at Genesis 41:43 and Solomon set on the king’s own mule at 1 Kings 1:33.

Over the crown the grammatical-historical and wesleyan-arminian readings part. Ellicott takes the Hebrew strictly — “the crown royal which is set upon his head” means, most literally, upon the horse’s head; his one hesitation is that there is no evidence of such a custom among the Persians, and he observes that neither the king in his reply nor the narrator in describing the event ever says Mordecai wore a crown. Clarke judges otherwise: interpreters are divided, he grants, but he thinks the royal crown for the man is meant, for why should Haman trouble to name the ordinary trappings of the royal steed? The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands with those who see a man’s crown intended, for Haman, he says, prescribes honours too great for any subject — the royal robe, the royal crown, the king’s own horse — that he might appear in all the pomp and grandeur of the king himself, wanting only the sceptre, the emblem of power he dared not ask.
9:
Haman’s design reaches its height in the public procession he prescribes, and here the witnesses begin already to hear the note of his undoing. The reformed John Gill passes quickly over the appointing of “one of the king’s most noble princes” to lead the honoured man, but Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, cannot let it pass without a cry: “Alas, poor Haman!” Never, he says, was the fable of the dog and the shadow more literally fulfilled — Haman gaped at the shadow and lost the substance, prescribing for another the very glory he thought to grasp for himself. The counsel he framed to exalt himself becomes, in his own mouth, the script of his mockery: every clause he adds to magnify the honour only deepens the humiliation about to be laid upon him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the words, referring “noble” and “the street of the city” back to their earlier uses in the book, at Esther 1:3 and Esther 4:6 — the same broad open square where the city’s public life was transacted, the very place before the king’s gate where Mordecai had so lately sat in his sackcloth and mourned, now to become the stage of his triumph and, though none yet knows it, of Haman’s shame. The word for the attendant, too, is the term used of the great princes of Persia, so that the pomp Haman sketches is drawn wholly from the court’s highest usages.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the proclamation Haman puts in the herald’s mouth — “Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour” — and finds in it the same intent as the cry that went before Joseph, “Bow the knee,” at Genesis 41:43; for every good subject will honour those whom the king honours. Then he lifts the scene to a higher key: shall not every good Christian likewise honour those whom the King of kings delights to honour, and call the saints upon the earth the excellent ones, as the psalmist does at Psalms 16:3? The lesson runs beneath the story, that honour freely rendered to God’s honoured ones is the mark of a loyal heart, whether in a Persian subject or a Christian. Haman, meanwhile, is heaping up in words a homage he supposes will crown his own head; and the witnesses, without yet naming the reversal, let the reader feel it gathering. The prince who was to walk before him, the robe, the horse, the proclamation through the square — every splendid particular he has invented will fall, within the hour, upon the head of the man he hates, and the herald’s cry he composed for his own praise will ring out for Mordecai the Jew.
10:
The blow falls in a single sentence: “Make haste, take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew.” The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry pictures the moment as a thunderclap. Had the king but said, as Haman expected, “Thou art the man,” the vizier would have had the fairest opening to press his errand and beg that Mordecai be hanged to grace the day; instead he is commanded to do all this honour himself, and to the very man he hated above all others and was at that hour designing to destroy. It is now to no purpose to move anything against Mordecai, whom the king delights to honour; the heart of the king, Henry notes with Proverbs 25:3, is unsearchable — though, he adds, it is not unchangeable.

The reformed John Gill fills in the errand from the Targum: Haman is to go to the royal wardrobe for the purple robe, and to the king’s stable for the horse that stands in the chief place, which the tradition even names Shiphregaz — for it was not unusual for kings to give a name to a favourite horse, as Alexander did to his Bucephalus. Adam Clarke, of the wesleyan-arminian school, measures the reverse: “O mortifying reverse of human fortune! How could Haman bear this?” The Targumist, he says, may speak according to nature when he tells that Haman besought the king to kill him rather than so degrade him. And Clarke draws the providence out: there is neither counsel nor wisdom against the Lord, and he who digs a pit for his neighbour is sure to fall into it himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notices the pointed phrase “the Jew.” Mordecai’s nationality would have been set down in the book of records, and its mention here quietly prepares the way for what follows: when Esther comes to urge her petition, she has already, in the king’s fresh goodwill toward one prominent member of the proscribed race, a friend at court she did not plant. So the witnesses read the verse as the pivot of the whole story. The honour Haman devised for himself is turned, by the king’s word, upon the head of his enemy; the man who came to ask a death is sent to proclaim a triumph; and the reader sees, in the king’s careless command, the sure hand of a God who is never named and never absent, overturning the proud in the very moment of their confidence.
11:
Now the dreadful office must be performed, and the witnesses watch the two men bear it. The reformed John Gill records the bare act: Haman took the robe from the wardrobe and the horse from the stable — and the crown too, no doubt, though it is not named, since the king had bidden that nothing fail of all that was spoken — and brought Mordecai on horseback through the most grand and public street of the city, proclaiming before him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch state the mortification at its root: a deeper humiliation Haman could not have suffered than to be obliged, by the king’s own command, publicly to pay the highest honour to the very man whose execution he had come that morning to procure.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the strange procession on both sides. Haman dares not dispute nor so much as seem to dislike the order, but with the greatest reluctance imaginable arrays his enemy and leads him through the streets; and it is hard to say, Henry muses, which of the two put the greater force upon himself — proud Haman in doing this honour, or humble Mordecai in accepting it. For Mordecai, he adds, valued Haman’s counterfeit respect no more than he had valued his concealed malice, and did no more cringe to him now than before; yet the honour was agreeable to him, not for its pomp, but as a token of the king’s favour that gave hope Esther might yet prevail for the reversing of the edict against the Jews.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns to the inward tumult the verse leaves unspoken, and calls it a grim and curious study to analyse Haman’s feelings at this juncture. Various thoughts were mingled there: self-reproach, perhaps, that he had so thoughtlessly been the cause of the display; a bitter hatred of his rival, now multiplied a thousandfold; and, above all, the plain knowledge that the game was played out and that he was ruined — for the subtler the brain, Ellicott remarks, the more truly he must have known it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets down the outward act, Keil the sting of it, Henry the mastery each man kept over himself, and Ellicott the ruin already legible to Haman’s own mind; and together they make the procession what the story means it to be — a triumph for the humble and a public foretaste of the proud man’s fall.
12:
The procession over, the two men part in opposite directions, and the witnesses read their whole characters in that parting. The reformed John Gill observes that Mordecai “came again to the king’s gate” — back to his post and office at court, not, as some imagine, to sackcloth and fasting; for he might now reasonably conclude that things were taking a turn in his favour and his people’s. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the return a lesson in humility unspoiled: Mordecai was not puffed up by his advancement but went straight back to his duty and minded his business as before, and honour is well bestowed on those who are not made proud and idle by it. Haman, by contrast, could not bear his part — to wait upon Mordecai, and at the very hour he had hoped to see him hanged, was enough to break such a proud heart; he hasted to his house mourning, with his head covered, as one who looked upon himself as already condemned. What harm had the stooping done him? Henry asks; and answers with a proverb of his own: that will break a proud man’s heart which would not so much as break a humble man’s sleep.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the same two postures. Adam Clarke sees Mordecai resume his former humble station while Haman, ashamed to look up, covers his face and runs home to hide — the covered head being, among most peoples of the earth, a sign of shame and grief alike. John Wesley marks that Mordecai returned to his former place, showing that as he was not overwhelmed by Haman’s threats, so neither was he puffed up by this honour; while Haman covered his head in token of his shame and grief at his disappointment, and at the great honour done to his abhorred adversary by his own hands and with his own public disgrace.

The grammatical-historical voices add the historian’s eye. Charles Ellicott notes that to the Eastern mind, which sees the vizier and the poor man continually change places, there was nothing startling in Mordecai’s quiet resumption of his humble post at the gate; the covered head, he agrees, is the token of mourning. Keil and Delitzsch fix the same gesture in the language of Scripture, the covering of the head a mark of deep confusion and grief such as meets us at Jeremiah 14:4 and 2 Samuel 15:30. The witnesses converge on one contrast: the honoured man walks back to his work unmoved, and the disgraced man hurries home undone.
13:
Haman flees home to his own, and the comfort he seeks turns to a sentence of doom. The reformed John Gill notes that he told Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had befallen him — how he was prevented from speaking his errand, and instead compelled to do to Mordecai the honour he had thought reserved for himself alone. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch report the household’s verdict: his wise men and Zeresh answered that if Mordecai, before whom he had begun to fall, were of the seed of the Jews, he should not prevail against him but would surely fall before him — and even as they spoke, the king’s chamberlains arrived to hurry Haman to Esther’s banquet.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen two details. John Wesley identifies the “wise men” as the magicians whom Haman, after the Persian manner, had called together to consult upon so strange an emergency. Adam Clarke notes that the Septuagint adds to their warning the words “for the living God is with him” — a sentiment, he observes, that could scarcely be expected from the mouth of such heathens as these. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the bitter turn in the single word “told,” the same used of Haman’s boasting at Esther 5:11: then the tale was one of swelling pride in what he had and hoped to be; now it is of bitter disappointment and bitter foreboding, unrelieved by any of the thoughts that blunt an honest sorrow. Poor comfort, Ellicott adds, the schemer gets from his own household — and he sets Zeresh’s chilling words beside the parting words of the wives of the martyrs John Rogers and Rowland Taylor in the days of the Marian persecution, to show how differently a fallen but blameless cause may be met at home.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry calls the wife and friends miserable comforters all: they did not counsel Haman to repent and seek Mordecai’s pardon, but foretold his ruin as fatal and unavoidable. Two things they foresaw — that he would not prevail to root out the Jews, heaven plainly fighting against him, and that he himself would fall; and two things they grounded it on. Mordecai was of the seed of the Jews, a holy and praying people in covenant with God, whom their enemies had often found formidable; and Haman had already begun to fall, and great court-favourites, once frowned upon, fall as fast as they rose. The contest between Michael and the dragon, Henry says, alluding to Revelation 12:7, will be no drawn battle; when God begins with the church’s enemies he will make an end, for as for God, his work is perfect.
14:
The scene closes on a summons that comes at the worst possible moment for Haman and the best for God’s design. The reformed John Gill sets the timing simply: while they were yet talking with him — his household still giving their gloomy opinion of the issue — the king’s chamberlains arrived. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks Haman’s reluctance: they hasted to bring him, who was now slow to go, by reason of the great dejection of his own mind; the man who the day before had gloried in his invitation to the queen’s table now drags himself toward it.

Adam Clarke, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, dwells on the dread that hung, all unknown, over the feast. There was a dreadful banquet before Haman of which he knew nothing, and he could have little appetite for the entertainment prepared for him at Esther’s palace. Here Clarke finds one grand design of the whole history laid bare: that he who lays a snare for the life of his neighbour is most likely to fall into it himself, for in the course of divine providence men generally meet with the very evils they have meant to inflict on others — exactly agreeable, he says, to the saying of our Lord, “With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again,” recorded at Matthew 7:2. The moral is not incidental, Clarke insists, but the very lesson the book was written to teach: the pit dug for another becomes the digger’s own grave, and the gallows raised for Mordecai will bear the weight of the man who built it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the timing as the very hinge of providence. Haman thought the summons seasonable, hoping the banquet would revive his drooping spirits and save his sinking honour; but it was seasonable in a sense he never suspected, for with his spirits now broken by so sore a disappointment he might the more easily be run down by Esther’s complaint against him the next day. The wisdom of God, Henry concludes, is seen in timing the means of his church’s deliverance so as to manifest his own glory — bringing the proud man low the night before the queen would plead, that the rescue of the Jews might come, unmistakably, from a hand higher than any at the Persian court. Haman goes to the feast a broken man and knows not that he goes to his sentence; the very invitation he had prized above measure the day before is become the summons to his ruin. So the chapter that opened with a king who could not sleep ends with a favourite who cannot eat; and between the two, without a word of his own name, the God of Israel has turned the whole engine of the empire to the saving of his people.
